runs.market_commentary:
Asian markets closed mixed overnight as the Nikkei 225 slid 0.29% to 63,108 — its third consecutive decline — weighed down by weaker-than-expected chip export data and a cautious Bank of Japan statement holding rates steady at 1.25% while signaling readiness to tighten further if wage growth sustains. Private PMI surveys showed factory activity across Asia continued to expand in October but growth slowed in major semiconductor exporters, reinforcing concerns about peak AI capex spending that drove last week's tech rout. The Hang Seng tracked losses in chip names while South Korea's KOSPI bounced modestly after SK Hynix surged nearly 5% on bargain-hunting following its own selloff.

European markets opened cautiously with the DAX virtually flat at 25,818 (-0.03%) and the FTSE 100 drifting to 10,725 (-0.19%) as a crude oil slide dragged BP and Shell lower. Oil prices fell toward $98/barrel as President Trump signaled the US-Iran conflict could be nearing a resolution, compressing the geopolitical risk premium that had propped up energy names for the past three weeks. European banks outperformed on the margin as bond yields stabilized, and defense names held up ahead of tomorrow's US midterm elections.

US pre-market futures are pointing to a relief bounce Monday morning after Wall Street's worst week in months — S&P 500 futures +0.50% to ~5,698, Nasdaq-100 futures +0.83% to ~20,056, and Dow futures +0.42% to ~42,780. The S&P 500 fell 2%, the Nasdaq 100 dropped 3.5%, and the Dow shed 1.1% on Friday amid broad AI spending fears. Today's catalyst mix is constructive: falling oil prices ease inflation concerns, Apple and Palantir report after the close, and Regeneron's Q3 beat (+13% pre-market) is lifting biotech sentiment. VIX remains elevated at 23.4, and the 10-year Treasury yield sits at 4.62%, suggesting markets have not fully cleared last week's anxiety. Oracle is a headwind, falling 3.3% after announcing a $10B equity offering.

runs.market_commentary:
Asian markets closed Friday's session under significant pressure, with the Nikkei 225 falling 2.06% to 63,290 as semiconductor and technology names led losses. The Nikkei decline was driven by broad-based tech selling following disappointing earnings from key U.S. semiconductor names, most notably Intel's catastrophic results which sent INTC down approximately 27-30% and triggered sector-wide contagion with AMD falling ~10% and the SOXL 3x semiconductor ETF losing over 30%. The Hang Seng also dipped sharply while Chinese tech shares faced pressure from PCB and chip supply chain concerns. This marks the third consecutive week of losses for the Nasdaq, which fell 2.0% on the week.

European markets showed more resilience on Friday with the FTSE 100 edging up a modest 0.07% to 10,729.78, buoyed by a 7% surge in AstraZeneca after the pharma giant beat Q3 EPS estimates ($2.79 actual vs. $2.59 expected) and reiterated full-year guidance — a rare bright spot in a week dominated by tech disappointments. The DAX closed down 0.85% at approximately 25,818 as German industrial sentiment and cost-of-living protests weighed on sentiment, though HSBC's upgrade of GE Vernova to Buy with a $1,100 target supported energy-transition names. McCormick's foods combination with Unilever also remains under UK CMA Phase 1 review through November 11.

U.S. pre-market futures on Sunday evening are pointing to a cautious start to the week, with S&P 500 futures near 7,614 (+0.01%), Dow futures around 51,928 (+0.02%), and Nasdaq futures at 28,543 (+0.03%). Markets are laser-focused on the upcoming FOMC rate decision — the Fed meets this week against a backdrop of a robust 3.4% Q3 GDP print (per the BEA advance estimate) and Atlanta Fed Q4 GDPNow of 3.3%, but three straight weeks of equity losses driven by disappointing AI-linked tech earnings. The Intel collapse, DoorDash's $17B Instacart acquisition, and record $175B November investment-grade bond issuance forecast are the dominant themes heading into Monday's open.

ideas.catalyst: Intel reported catastrophic Q3 earnings, sending shares down 26-30% in pre-market trading as the company's data center and PC chip businesses continue to lose share to AMD and NVIDIA.
ideas.thesis: Intel's fundamental competitive position has deteriorated irreversibly in both PC and server markets, with AMD eating client share and NVIDIA dominating AI accelerators where Intel is years behind. The magnitude of the earnings miss and -30% reaction signals further institutional selling as fund managers reposition away from legacy semis; even the KGI upgrade to $95 and BofA's neutral at $100 suggest limited upside and reflect capitulation rather than conviction.
ideas.key_risk: Buyout speculation or activist involvement could trigger a violent short-squeeze rally in a heavily shorted name.

runs.market_commentary:
Asian markets closed sharply lower on Friday (Oct 30) as Intel's catastrophic earnings rippled through global technology sectors. Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 2.06%, settling at 63,326, its steepest single-day decline since June, driven by heavy selling in semiconductor-exposed names like Tokyo Electron and Advantest. The yen strengthened on safe-haven flows while the Hang Seng also declined. The rout began after Intel reported Q3 results with a deeply negative Q4 forecast and cash flow warning, raising broader fears about AI capex sustainability.

European markets demonstrated surprising resilience on Friday despite the Wall Street contagion. The DAX closed up 1.31% at 26,039.68, supported by energy majors benefiting from Brent crude pushing to $118 — a six-month high — and financials outperforming. The FTSE 100 added 0.26% to 10,722.07, cushioned by UK oil and gas heavyweights including Shell and BP. The divergence between European and US markets reflected sector composition: European indices are more energy- and financials-heavy, insulating them from US semiconductor weakness.

US equities recorded their worst session since June on Friday. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.82%. Intel shed 28.6% — its worst day since 1974 — after Q4 guidance came in far below consensus and management flagged negative free cash flow. Alphabet also missed Q3 EPS estimates amid heavy AI capex scrutiny. As of Saturday pre-market, futures are tentatively stabilizing: S&P 500 futures +0.01%, Nasdaq +0.03%, Dow +0.02%, suggesting a potential relief bounce Monday but no meaningful recovery catalyst yet. Bitcoin tumbled to $77,000 on Binance-related security news, adding to risk-off sentiment. US Q3 GDP printed at 3.4% but inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target, keeping rate-cut hopes subdued.
